flashcards.a: X -> Y means every row sharing the same X value must have the same Y value - knowing X determines Y. Every normal form is defined purely in terms of which FDs are/aren't allowed relative to candidate keys.
Atomic values and no repeating groups - no comma-separated lists in a column, no col1/col2 repeating-group pairs.

flashcards.q: What does 2NF forbid, and when is it automatically satisfied?
flashcards.a: Forbids partial dependencies - every non-key attribute must depend on the WHOLE key, not just part of it. Automatically satisfied by any table with a single-column primary key; only a real constraint with composite keys.
Transitive dependencies - a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the key (key -> A -> B is the violation shape).

flashcards.q: What loophole does BCNF close that 3NF leaves open?
flashcards.a: 3NF only forbids non-key attributes transitively depending on the key; BCNF additionally requires every determinant of every non-trivial FD to be a candidate key - closing the case where a determinant is part of one candidate key but not a full candidate key itself, in a table with overlapping candidate keys.

course_enrollment(student_id, course_id, instructor), key (student_id, course_id), with course_id -> instructor. This is 3NF (instructor isn't reached via a non-key attribute) but violates BCNF since course_id alone doesn't determine student_id, so it isn't a candidate key yet is a determinant.

flashcards.q: Why isn't BCNF decomposition always dependency-preserving?
flashcards.a: Decomposing to BCNF can split a functional dependency across two tables such that checking it requires rejoining them, losing the ability to enforce that constraint with a single-table check - unlike 3NF decomposition, which is guaranteed to preserve dependencies.

flashcards.q: What does 4NF forbid, define a multi-valued dependency.
flashcards.a: X ->> Y: the set of Y values associated with X is independent of any other attribute in the table. 4NF forbids combining two independent multi-valued facts about one entity into a single table, which forces storing their cross product.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a 4NF violation and its fix.
flashcards.a: product_tags_warehouses(product_id, tag, warehouse_id) where tags and warehouses are independent - a product with 3 tags and 2 warehouses needs 6 rows instead of 5. Fix: split into product_tags(product_id, tag) and product_warehouses(product_id, warehouse_id).

flashcards.q: Name the three classic anomalies with one-line definitions.
flashcards.a: Update anomaly: duplicated fact updated in some but not all rows -> inconsistency. Insert anomaly: can't record one entity's fact until an unrelated fact is also available. Delete anomaly: deleting a row to remove one fact accidentally destroys a different, unrelated fact stored in the same row.

flashcards.q: What two things must be true for denormalization to be a sound engineering decision, not a shortcut?
flashcards.a: You must be able to name (1) the exact anomaly being reintroduced, and (2) the specific consistency mechanism keeping the duplicate correct (trigger, write-through, CDC sync, or an explicitly accepted staleness window). No mechanism means it's a scheduled bug, not a decision.

flashcards.q: What's the practical default normal form for OLTP schema design?
flashcards.a: 3NF (or BCNF where they diverge) - eliminates essentially all common anomalies with a manageable number of tables. 4NF/5NF only worth pursuing when a genuine multi-valued-dependency problem is actually identified.

flashcards.q: How do you empirically check whether a candidate functional dependency actually holds in real data?
flashcards.a: Group rows by the candidate determinant's value(s) and check whether every group has a single consistent dependent value - any group with more than one distinct value violates the FD in the sampled data (though absence of violation doesn't logically prove the FD holds universally).

flashcards.q: Why do star schemas/OLAP dimensional models count as a legitimate default case for denormalization?
flashcards.a: The read pattern (few large scans, rare updates to dimension data) makes anomaly risk low and join-avoidance benefit high - this is the clearest case where denormalization is a first-class design tool, not an exception requiring special justification.
